newsitem.title: USA: Nuclear plants must cut jobs, boost safety - execs.
newsitem.headline: Nuclear plants must cut jobs, boost safety - execs.

text.p: Nuclear plant owners must cut jobs and other costs while improving plant performance and safety to stay in business as power markets are opened to competition, industry officials said Thursday.

Fifteen nuclear plants in the states that are most likely to have open power markets by 2000 will be unable to survive unless they cut costs, Steven Specker, president of General Electric Co's GE Nuclear Energy predicted.

Eight of the 15 uncompetitive plants need to save up to $30 million, four need to save $30 million to $60 million, two need to save up to $100 million, and one needs to cut costs by more than $100 million to survive, he said. "Competitiveness is going to be driven by staffing levels," he said at the Nuclear Energy Institute's annual meeting.

PECO Energy Co CEO Corbin McNeill said utilities should focus on four key issues: developing a safety culture that ensured reliable operations, shaving operations and maintenance costs, consolidating single unit operations to cut overhead costs, and arresting declines in performance.
"The bigger an entity is, the more you can sustain the loss of one plant for some period of time," he said.

"If that plant goes down for a short period of time, your cash flow is so negative, you have to balance that risk with the marketplace," he said later, commenting on how PECO evaluates whether to buy a nuclear plant or not.

Jessica Tuchman Mathews, president of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, said the industry would be better off if the government gave up trying to build a permanent dump for spent nuclear fuel from power plants.
The United States should focus on building underground retrievable storage for radioactive waste, instead of wasting time trying to find a place to bury the spent fuel safely for 10,000 years.
She called the 10,000 year requirement "nonsense technically" and "unattainable".

The industry has been pressing the government to build a temporary storage facility for spent nuclear fuel so that utilities can start moving the radioactive waste off their sites before the government has built a permanent dump.

Under law, the government was supposed to start taking the waste by the end of January 1998, but the Clinton administration has said it does not expect to have a place to put the spent fuel until 2010 at the earliest.
